article_title: Advancing to Completion: Increasing Degree Attainment by Improving Graduation Rates and Closing Gaps for Hispanic Students
citation: Mary Nguyen, Erin Ward Bibo, and Jennifer Engle. (2012). Advancing to Completion: Increasing degree attainment by improving graduation rates and closing gaps for Hispanic students. The Education Trust. https://www.collegeresults.org
title: Educational Opportunity Program (EOP) at Stony Brook University
description: EOP is a state-sponsored access-and-support program at Stony Brook serving nearly 600 low-income students and students of color whose high school preparation was incomplete. It provides "a five-week summer 'boot camp' program, personal counseling and academic advising at least three times a semester, and a mandatory study skill workshop" including an academic success contract. The report reports EOP students graduate at higher rates than other Stony Brook students despite entering less prepared.
requirements: State sponsorship for economically disadvantaged students with college potential
Intensive advising and support services staffed to build a familial community
constraints: The report attributes the graduation comparison to Stony Brook's Office of Institutional Research, not an independent evaluation
examples: Stony Brook completely closed an 11.5 percentage point Hispanic-white graduation gap from 2004 to 2010 while EOP students graduated at higher rates than peers
key_sources: Mary Nguyen, Erin Ward Bibo, and Jennifer Engle. (2012). Advancing to Completion: Increasing degree attainment by improving graduation rates and closing gaps for Hispanic students. The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED535510

article_title: 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders about Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School
citation: The Education Trust; Equal Opportunity Schools. (2023). 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders About Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School. https://edtrust.org
title: EOS Student Insight Card
description: The Student Insight Card is Equal Opportunity Schools' flagship tool for identifying students for advanced coursework. It "includes data about students’ interests and aspirations — such as expressed desire to enroll, student motivation, and recommendations from trusted school staff" so this data factors into academic opportunity and enrollment decisions. EOS states it "transforms the definition of readiness schools use to determine access to advanced courses."
requirements: Schools must factor the card's interest, motivation, and trusted-staff-recommendation data into enrollment decisions about academic opportunity
target_learners: Black and Latino high school students
target_learning_goals: Access to and success in advanced STEM coursework
examples: The brief recommends the card as a multiple-measures identification tool so students are not gated by a single test score or teacher recommendation
key_sources: The Education Trust; Equal Opportunity Schools. (2023). 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders About Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627984

article_title: 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders about Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School
citation: The Education Trust; Equal Opportunity Schools. (2023). 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders About Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School. https://edtrust.org
title: EOS Opportunity Chart
description: The EOS Opportunity Chart is a data tool that "allows schools and districts to see and report disaggregated course enrollments relative to the demographics of their school population to see where gaps exist." It supports the brief's first question about goals and monitoring data, enabling regular public reporting of seats, enrollment, and success in advanced courses across school levels.
requirements: Regular, public reports with detailed, disaggregated data around seats, enrollment, and success in advanced courses
target_learners: Black and Latino students across elementary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Monitoring equitable access to advanced coursework
examples: The brief lists the Opportunity Chart under look-fors for leaders' goals and progress-monitoring data on advanced course access
key_sources: The Education Trust; Equal Opportunity Schools. (2023). 5 Questions to Ask District and School Leaders About Access to Advanced STEM Coursework in High School. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED627984

article_title: AI Literacy in Secondary Education: Framework, Assessment, and Professional Development in the Ukrainian Context
citation: Marienko, M. V., Markova, O. M., & Semerikov, S. O. (2026). AI literacy in secondary education: framework, assessment, and professional development in the Ukrainian context. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 10, 100605. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100605
title: Curated catalog of 22 EOSC AI services mapped to secondary school subjects
description: Study 4 systematically searched the EOSC Marketplace using AI- and ML-related keywords, filtering candidates against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria with independent dual assessment and consensus, producing a curated catalog for educator reference. The analysis found that "Systematic analysis identified 22 EOSC AI services applicable to secondary education." Services were mapped to six subject areas, with biology (7 services) and geography (6) accounting for the largest share, reflecting the European research infrastructure's emphasis on environmental and earth sciences.
requirements: Services had to meet inclusion criteria of AI/ML functionality, educational applicability, and accessibility
constraints: Services that were purely research-oriented without educational potential or inaccessible without institutional affiliation were excluded
target_learning_goals: subject-specific AI integration in biology, geography, chemistry, physics, and mathematics instruction
examples: Mapped services include AI-GeoSpecies and GBIF hosted portals for species identification in biology, and Copernicus Data Space and WEkEO for spatial data analysis in geography
key_sources: Marienko, M. V., Markova, O. M., & Semerikov, S. O. (2026). AI literacy in secondary education: framework, assessment, and professional development in the Ukrainian context. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 10, 100605. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100605

article_title: Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive #x0022;Quantified Self #x0022;
citation: Kai Kunze, Masakazu Iwamura, Koichi Kise, Seiichi Uchida, and Shinichiro Omachi. (2013). Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive “Quantified Self.” Computer, IEEE Computer Society, October 2013. http://kaikunze.de/papers/2013Kunze-1.pdf
title: Two mobile eye-gaze recording methods: electrooculography and infrared stereo eye tracking
description: The article describes two promising methods for recording eye gaze in real-life mobile settings. Electrooculography (EOG) measures potential changes as the eye moves as a cornea-retina dipole; with this technique "it's possible to recognize reading and other eye movements in realistic everyday scenarios". The alternative tracks gaze with infrared light and stereo cameras, "provides potentially higher accuracy but requires more processing power", inferring motion from iris shape and local face features.
requirements: EOG requires electrodes touching the skin near the eye; infrared tracking requires cameras, infrared LEDs, and more processing power
constraints: EOG electrodes can be uncomfortable even when embedded in eyeglass frames; commercial mobile eye trackers are still quite expensive
target_learning_goals: mobile monitoring of reading and cognitive activity
examples: A cheap 3D-printed open source mobile gaze tracker (OMG!) was shown at the MobileHCI conference, and researchers have experimented with front cameras on tablets and phones for low-fidelity gaze detection
key_sources: Kai Kunze, Masakazu Iwamura, Koichi Kise, Seiichi Uchida, and Shinichiro Omachi. (2013). Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive “Quantified Self.” Computer, IEEE Computer Society, October 2013. http://kaikunze.de/papers/2013Kunze-1.pdf

article_title: Developing an e-learning course on the use of PRO measures in oncological practice: health care professionals' preferences for learning content and methods.
citation: Sztankay Monika, Wintner Lisa M., Roggendorf Sigrid, Nordhausen Thomas, Dirven Linda, Taphoorn Martin J. B., Verdonck-de Leeuw Irma M., Velikova Galina, Bottomley Andrew, Kulis Dagmara, Kachel Timo, Schmidt Heike. (2021). Developing an e-learning course on the use of PRO measures in oncological practice: health care professionals’ preferences for learning content and methods. Supportive Care in Cancer. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00520-021-06676-x
title: E-learning course on the use of EORTC PRO measures in oncological practice (eight modular topics with mixed presentation formats)
description: A web-based e-learning course under development to support health care professionals in the routine use of EORTC PRO assessments in oncology, designed via a user-centred, participatory approach following the CeHRes Roadmap. Its final planned structure (Table 3) comprises eight modules — from "Basic information on PROs in clinical routine" to "Self-management recommendations for patients based on PROs" — each combining written information and graphics, with topic-specific practical examples, interactive case vignettes for communication, and "Interactive components to enhance knowledge-practice transfer"; blended learning, certification and tests of learning progress are to be considered.
requirements: Digital training tools must take "the clinical realities of limited human resources, time and funding into account"; a participatory approach during each stage of development is recommended to maximise acceptance.
constraints: The article notes awareness of the limitations of e-learning, including individual or structural barriers for its use.
target_learners: Oncology health care professionals (physicians, nurses, psycho-oncologists, allied health professionals, IT specialists)
target_learning_goals: Competences in using EORTC PRO measures in clinical routine: interpreting PRO data, integrating PROs into patient communication, PRO-based clinical actions, and implementing routine PRO assessment
examples: The final selection (Table 3) assigns written information and graphics to all eight topics, adds interactive case vignettes for communication, examples of clinical action based on PRO results, and video clips of patients using self-management recommendations.
key_sources: Sztankay Monika, Wintner Lisa M., Roggendorf Sigrid, Nordhausen Thomas, Dirven Linda, Taphoorn Martin J. B., Verdonck-de Leeuw Irma M., Velikova Galina, Bottomley Andrew, Kulis Dagmara, Kachel Timo, Schmidt Heike. (2021). Developing an e-learning course on the use of PRO measures in oncological practice: health care professionals’ preferences for learning content and methods. Supportive Care in Cancer. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00520-021-06676-x

article_title: Construct, content and face validity of the eoSim laparoscopic simulator on advanced suturing tasks.
citation: Leijte Erik, Arts Elke, Witteman Bart, Jakimowicz Jack, De Blaauw Ivo, Botden Sanne. (2019). Construct, content and face validity of the eoSim laparoscopic simulator on advanced suturing tasks. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-018-06652-3
title: eoSim augmented reality laparoscopic simulator with instrument tracking
description: The eoSim is a relatively low-cost (£699–£1298 at the time of writing), low-weight, mobile inanimate laparoscopic simulator by EoSurgical ltd. with an internally mounted high-definition camera and Surgtrac software that tracks instrument tips via coloured markings. The article states it "shows performance parameters after each task while working with real instruments", making it an augmented reality simulator providing parametric feedback independent of the task performed. In this study it recorded time, path length, off-screen percentage, speed, working area, acceleration and smoothness across three suturing tasks.
requirements: A 15-in. laptop with the recommended specifications and the eoSurgical Surgtrac software installed, connected to the tracking camera via USB 2.0
constraints: The installed webcam's focus could not be manually adjusted to the user's preference, which the authors report could cause frustration and affect opinion and performance
Construct validity could not be established on all separate parameters; acceleration and smoothness are calculated from speed and the authors state they should not be used for assessment purposes
examples: 104 participants at three Dutch hospitals and two national conferences performed an intracorporeal suturing task, an upside-down needle transfer and an anastomosis needle transfer on the eoSim
key_sources: Leijte Erik, Arts Elke, Witteman Bart, Jakimowicz Jack, De Blaauw Ivo, Botden Sanne. (2019). Construct, content and face validity of the eoSim laparoscopic simulator on advanced suturing tasks. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-018-06652-3

article_title: Learning end-of-life care within a constructivist model: Undergraduate nursing students' experiences.
citation: Van der Wath, A.E. & Du Toit, P.H., 2015, 'Learning end-of-life care within a constructivist model: Undergraduate nursing students' experiences', Curationis 38(2), Art. #1537. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v38i2.1537
title: Nurse educators should plan end-of-life learning opportunities that raise emotional awareness and provide opportunities for value clarification
description: From the study's practical implications, nurse educators should "plan learning opportunities that will facilitate learning about end-of-life- care to raise students' emotional awareness and provide opportunities for students to clarify personal values about death and dying". The principle rests on the study's findings that experiential opportunities triggered emotional experiences and supported value clarification. Educators are also advised to use creative methods ensuring students participate and use their senses.
requirements: Purposefully designed experiential learning opportunities rather than knowledge-and-skills-only teaching; feedback on students' learning experiences
constraints: Findings derive from a single qualitative study; the authors note quantitative data and assessment of real-life clinical encounters were lacking
target_learning_goals: emotional awareness of death and dying, value clarification, and end-of-life care competency
examples: The module's four learning opportunities combined creative group presentations with open discussion and LEARN-guided written reflection
key_sources: Van der Wath, A.E. & Du Toit, P.H., 2015, 'Learning end-of-life care within a constructivist model: Undergraduate nursing students' experiences', Curationis 38(2), Art. #1537. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v38i2.1537
